paragraphs: Automated theorem provers must choose among many possible tactics at every step. As proofs become longer, these choices produce an enormous search space. Some candidate tactics accomplish essentially the same thing, while others fail during execution. Trying all of them spends resources without exploring proportionately more useful possibilities.

3D-Prover learns representations of tactics from synthetic data collected during earlier proof attempts. These representations capture what a tactic does to the proving environment, its likelihood of succeeding, and its execution time. A filtering mechanism then uses determinantal point processes to select candidates that combine quality with semantic diversity. The selection therefore considers both individual usefulness and how much candidates overlap.

The authors augment existing open-source proving language models and evaluate them on miniF2F and LeanDojo. They report higher proof rates alongside improvements in tactic success, execution time, and diversity. The contribution is a way to spend proof-search resources more effectively, designed to work alongside an underlying tactic generator.
neurips-2025-3d-prover-diversity-driven-.tldr: 3D-Prover improves proof search by selecting promising tactics that also explore meaningfully different possibilities.

paragraphs: Graph generators create data containing entities and the connections between them. Their outputs can carry unfairness through both connection patterns and attributes attached to individual nodes. The paper argues that existing fair graph generation methods mainly address structural bias, leaving node feature bias insufficiently addressed. Many also generate graphs sequentially, making their behavior sensitive to the ordering used.

FairGEM is a one-shot generation framework designed to mitigate both sources of bias together. Its central contribution is to treat the fairness of graph structure and node attributes as parts of the same generation problem. This matters because improving one component alone can leave the other component biased.

The authors provide theoretical results establishing stronger fairness guarantees than existing models while preserving generation quality. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets also report improvements in both fairness and output quality. Together, these findings support the framework's joint treatment of the two biases within the generation settings studied.
neurips-2025-a-unified-framework-for-fai.tldr: FairGEM jointly addresses bias in graph connections and node features, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements in fairness and generation quality.

paragraphs: Active target discovery asks where to collect the next observation when measurements are expensive and the search budget is limited. Methods using generative models can exploit learned expectations about where targets are likely to occur. Those expectations become less useful when there is too little data, or collecting enough data to learn them is prohibitively costly.

This paper develops a framework for discovery when the initial prior provides little guidance. Its design draws inspiration from neuroscience, and the title emphasizes permanent and transient memory. The framework is interpretable, allowing its sampling decisions to be understood. The authors also establish a guarantee that prior estimates improve monotonically as new observations arrive.

Experiments and ablation studies cover several domains, including species distribution modeling and remote sensing, and show substantial improvements over baseline approaches. The practical significance is the ability to improve exploration from observations even when a strong learned prior is unavailable at the outset.
neurips-2025-active-target-discovery-und.tldr: The proposed interpretable discovery framework improves sampling from initially uninformative priors as observations accumulate.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to learn actions that satisfy safety requirements without interacting directly with the environment during learning. Across multiple tasks, those requirements can differ in both type and permitted cost. Existing Decision Transformer approaches struggle with this variation, particularly when several constraints must be handled together.

CoPDT introduces two mechanisms that make constraints central to the model's decisions. A prompt encoder uses sparse binary cost signals to identify the relevant constraints. A second mechanism dynamically generates return-to-go inputs from those constraints and their safety budgets. These inputs express the future return being sought, replacing reliance on heuristically specified targets.

On the OSRL benchmark, the authors report improved efficiency and safety compliance across multiple tasks. CoPDT satisfies safety constraints in more than twice as many tasks as the compared leading Decision Transformer methods. This result supports adapting the model's conditioning to each constraint configuration and budget, without establishing unrestricted safety guarantees.
neurips-2025-adaptable-safe-policy-learn.tldr: CoPDT conditions offline policy learning on identified constraints and safety budgets, improving safety compliance across multiple tasks.

paragraphs: A multi-index model takes a high-dimensional input but depends only on its projection into a smaller subspace. The paper studies how difficult it is to learn such models under Gaussian inputs, including when labels are adversarially corrupted. The goal is accurate prediction under squared loss with formal learning guarantees.

The proposed algorithm applies to bounded-variation models whose relevant structure can be distinguished through moments of sufficiently low degree across projections. Its dependence on input dimension grows with that degree, while dependence on the relevant subspace dimension and desired accuracy can be much larger. The authors obtain improved accuracy dependence in realizable and independent-noise settings.

A nearly matching lower bound applies to statistical-query learners when distinguishing moments are absent at a given degree. This provides evidence for the algorithm's dimensional efficiency within that computational framework. An application yields an efficient learner for positively homogeneous Lipschitz models, including qualifying ReLU networks, with complexity independent of network size.
neurips-2025-algorithms-and-sq-lower-bou.tldr: The paper gives robust learning algorithms for structured multi-index models and statistical-query lower bounds that nearly match their dependence on input dimension.

paragraphs: Large reasoning models produce an intermediate thinking process before answering, but this does not automatically make them effective judges of translation quality. The paper systematically studies that role and identifies three difficulties: evaluation materials need to suit the models, simple examples can trigger excessive thinking, and scoring mechanisms can lead to overly generous assessments.

The authors address these issues by training the models on synthetic reasoning trajectories designed to resemble human evaluation. This calibrates how they think about translations. The approach targets the reasoning process itself, seeking to make the evaluation more effective while reducing the amount of thinking required.

Experiments on the WMT24 Metrics benchmarks cover models with 7 billion to 32 billion parameters. The method reduces thinking budgets by approximately a factor of 35 while improving evaluation performance. One reported example is an 8.7-point correlation improvement for R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. These findings show that tailored reasoning calibration can improve both efficiency and translation judgment in the tested models.
neurips-2025-are-large-reasoning-models-.tldr: Training reasoning models on synthetic evaluation trajectories improves translation judgments while sharply reducing their thinking budgets.

paragraphs: Test-time discovery asks a model to recognize emerging categories during use while retaining its ability to handle familiar ones. Memory-based approaches can store observations without additional training, but their fixed representations may fail to separate unfamiliar categories effectively. DAA addresses this by making the representation adaptable.

The Discrepancy-Amplifying Adapter is trained to increase feature differences between known and unknown classes. Training uses simulated unknown categories and a warm-up strategy to improve discrimination. At test time, a Short-Term Memory Renewal mechanism keeps a queue for unknown classes and selectively updates their representative prototypes using recent samples judged reliable.

The adapter also continues learning through a self-supervised objective, supporting retention of known categories while sharpening distinctions among emerging ones. Experiments report improved novel-class discovery together with adaptability and stability. The approach matters because it combines a changing representation with refreshed memory: both how observations are described and which observations represent new categories can evolve during use.
neurips-2025-daa-amplifying-unknown-disc.tldr: DAA combines an adaptive feature module with refreshed short-term memory to improve discovery of new classes during inference.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification uses a small labeled support set to classify new query examples. Changes in environments or capture devices can create differences between the two sets, as well as variation within each set. The paper combines these difficulties into a challenge called Dual Support Query Shift.

DUAL addresses the challenge by improving features before aligning their distributions. A repairer network learns from perturbed examples and adversarially generated hard examples to help produce cleaner representations. A two-stage optimal transport procedure then aligns support instances, brings same-class representations closer together, and uses query examples as anchors. A negative entropy regularizer is part of this alignment procedure.

The authors provide a theoretical bound and compare the method with ten leading baselines on three image datasets. They report an average performance improvement of 25.66%. The result supports the central idea that feature repair and distribution alignment can reinforce each other when shifts occur both within and between the available example sets.
neurips-2025-dual-alignment-framework-fo.tldr: DUAL combines feature repair and two-stage distribution alignment to improve few-shot classification under shifts within and between example sets.

paragraphs: An ensemble of regression models can express uncertainty through disagreement among its component predictions. Epistemic uncertainty concerns what the model does not yet know, making it useful for deciding which additional observations to acquire. Estimating it with Monte Carlo sampling can, however, be computationally expensive.

Pairwise Epistemic Estimators use distances between ensemble components to estimate this uncertainty. The approach builds on pairwise-distance estimators that establish bounds on entropy, a measure of uncertainty. The authors use those bounds to enhance Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement, connecting a more efficient uncertainty calculation to the selection of informative training examples.

Experiments include one-dimensional sinusoidal regression and the Pendulum, Hopper, Ant, and Humanoid benchmarks. The authors report uncertainty estimation up to 100 times faster than sample-based Monte Carlo methods and stronger performance in higher dimensions. Their active-learning results show advantages over baselines in high-dimensional regression, supporting the value of pairwise comparisons when repeated sampling becomes costly.
neurips-2025-epistemic-uncertainty-estim.tldr: Pairwise comparisons between ensemble components enable faster epistemic uncertainty estimation and improve high-dimensional regression active learning.

paragraphs: Functional classification works with inputs that are entire functions, creating an infinite-dimensional learning problem. This paper asks how to classify such inputs while keeping disparity across subpopulations below a chosen threshold. Standard tools become difficult to use because density ratios may be unavailable and posterior probabilities can be intractable.

The authors develop a unified framework for this setting and introduce Fair Functional Linear Discriminant Analysis, or Fair-FLDA. The algorithm targets homoscedastic Gaussian processes, which share a covariance structure, and applies group-specific decision thresholds as a post-processing step. Those thresholds provide a way to adjust fairness in the classifier's decisions.

Under weak structural assumptions on the eigenspace, the paper establishes guarantees controlling both fairness and excess classification risk. Its risk analysis also includes standard FLDA as a special case. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets complement the theory, supporting the practicality of the algorithm within the functional-data setting and assumptions studied.
neurips-2025-fairness-aware-bayes-optima.tldr: Fair-FLDA uses group-specific thresholds to control disparity in functional classification, with fairness and risk guarantees under stated structural assumptions.

paragraphs: Data attribution for text-to-image models asks which training images most influenced a particular generated output. Existing approaches can require substantial computation for every output being investigated. That repeated cost makes attribution difficult to apply at the scale of large image generators and their training collections.

The paper transfers the behavior of a slow, unlearning-based attribution method into a learned feature space. Once this representation is available, deployment becomes an efficient retrieval problem: indexing and search identify influential training images without rerunning the expensive attribution procedure for each query. The learned representation carries the information needed for this faster search.

Evaluations cover medium-scale models trained on MSCOCO and large Stable Diffusion models trained on LAION. The authors report better or competitive attribution performance in a few seconds, with speedups ranging from 2,500 to 400,000 times over existing methods. These results support distillation as a route toward practical attribution for large text-to-image systems.
neurips-2025-fast-data-attribution-for-t.tldr: Distilling expensive attribution into a searchable feature space identifies influential training images in seconds.

paragraphs: Research on fake images is divided across deepfakes, image manipulation, AI-generated images, and manipulated documents. These areas often use separate datasets, software, and evaluation rules, making cross-domain comparisons difficult. ForensicHub brings them into a shared benchmark and codebase for detecting fake images and locating manipulated regions.

Its modular, configuration-driven architecture makes datasets, transformations, models, and evaluators interchangeable. The project implements ten baseline models, including three reproduced from scratch, and introduces benchmarks for AI-generated images and documents. Adapters connect existing DeepfakeBench and IMDLBenCo resources. A shared forensic fusion evaluation protocol supports training and testing across different tasks.

In total, the resource includes four tasks, 23 datasets, 42 baseline models, six backbones, and eleven GPU-accelerated image-level and pixel-level metrics. It supports sixteen types of cross-domain evaluation. The authors also derive eight actionable insights about models, datasets, and evaluation. Its main contribution is shared experimental infrastructure that makes previously separated forensic research easier to compare and combine.
neurips-2025-forensichub-a-unified-bench.tldr: ForensicHub unifies datasets, models, and evaluation across four domains of fake-image detection and localization.

paragraphs: GS2E creates synthetic event-stream data from sparse photographs of real scenes taken from multiple viewpoints. Existing synthesis methods commonly depend on dense RGB videos, which can restrict viewpoint diversity and introduce geometric inconsistency. Dedicated hardware capture offers another route, but can be expensive and difficult to scale.

The method first reconstructs photorealistic static scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It then runs a physically informed event simulation pipeline that combines adaptive trajectory interpolation with modeling of event contrast thresholds. These components generate temporally dense streams under varied motion and lighting while keeping the events aligned with the reconstructed scene geometry.

The resulting large-scale dataset is evaluated through event-based 3D reconstruction experiments. The authors report superior generalization and argue for its value as an event-vision benchmark. The contribution is a connection between sparse real-world RGB capture and controllable event simulation, with reconstructed static scenes providing a consistent geometric basis for generating diverse observations.
neurips-2025-gs2e-gaussian-splatting-is-.tldr: GS2E turns sparse multi-view photographs into geometrically consistent synthetic event streams using Gaussian Splatting and physically informed simulation.

paragraphs: Transferring an appearance described by an image or text onto a 3D asset becomes difficult when the source and target have substantially different geometry. The authors find that directly applying a 3D generative model does not produce appealing results in this setting. GuideFlow3D instead steers generation toward the desired transfer.

The method uses a pretrained rectified flow model without additional training. During sampling, it periodically applies guidance expressed as a differentiable loss. The authors explore guidance based on part-aware appearance losses and self-similarity. This gives the sampling process an explicit signal about which appearance relationships it should preserve or reproduce.

Experiments show successful transfer of textures and geometric details, with qualitative and quantitative improvements over baselines. The paper also argues that traditional metrics struggle with local detail and geometrically dissimilar inputs when ground truth is absent. It therefore uses GPT-based output rankings, with a user study supporting their human-like assessment. Extensions to other diffusion models and guidance functions are presented as possibilities.
neurips-2025-guideflow3d-optimization-gu.tldr: GuideFlow3D periodically guides a pretrained generative model to transfer appearance onto 3D assets with substantially different geometry.

paragraphs: In a heterophilic graph, connected nodes often have different labels. A common design rule uses low-pass filtering for graphs with similar neighbors and high-pass filtering for graphs with dissimilar neighbors. This paper finds that the relationship is more complicated: useful filter responses vary across frequency components and do not track heterophily in a strictly monotonic way.

The theoretical analysis examines how graph heterophily relates to the average frequency response of graph neural networks. Its findings motivate filters that adapt to the graph's relationships. HeroFilter extracts information across the heterophily spectrum, then adaptively mixes the representations that carry useful signals.

Across homophilic and heterophilic graphs, the authors report accuracy improvements of up to 9.2% over leading baselines. The significance is that a single measure of neighbor-label similarity does not straightforwardly determine the best spectral response. Learning how to combine information across that spectrum can improve performance across the different graph settings tested.
neurips-2025-herofilter-adaptive-spectra.tldr: HeroFilter adaptively combines graph spectral information because useful filtering behavior does not vary monotonically with heterophily.

paragraphs: Neural routing solvers can struggle when applied to problems with different sizes or distributions from their training data. The paper links this difficulty to learning reusable structural principles of good routes. It identifies a pattern called Purity Law: an edge's prevalence in optimal solutions grows exponentially with the sparsity of nearby vertices.

The authors support this relationship with statistical and theoretical analysis across diverse instances. It describes a consistent preference associated with local sparsity within globally optimal routes. They then introduce Purity Policy Optimization, a training method that aligns characteristics of a neural solver's constructed solutions with this structural pattern.

Experiments show that the training approach can be integrated with popular neural routing solvers and substantially improve their generalization. The reported gains require no additional computation during inference. The contribution therefore connects an analyzed property of optimal routes to the training process, giving solvers a structural guide that can remain useful across changes in problem scale and distribution.
neurips-2025-purity-law-for-neural-routi.tldr: Purity Policy Optimization trains routing solvers to follow a structural pattern in optimal routes, improving generalization without extra inference computation.

paragraphs: Preference-based reward models learn which responses people favor, but can attach excessive importance to incidental features. Verbosity, agreeable tone, and sycophancy may correlate with preference labels without representing the intended objective. Optimizing against such a model can encourage policies to exploit those shortcuts for higher reward.

PRISM treats these behaviors through a common invariance-based approach. Drawing on kernel theory, it learns group-invariant kernels with feature maps through a closed-form learning objective. The aim is to reduce the reward model's dependence on shortcut features, addressing the broader pattern rather than investigating each undesirable behavior separately.

Experiments across several benchmarks show consistent improvements in reward-model accuracy on out-of-distribution tasks. The authors also report reduced shortcut dependence in downstream policy models. This connects the method's effect on reward prediction to the behavior of models trained using those rewards. The results support invariance as a useful strategy for making preference-based alignment less vulnerable to spurious training correlations.
neurips-2025-rectifying-shortcut-behavio.tldr: PRISM uses invariant reward representations to reduce reliance on spurious preference cues and improve out-of-distribution reward accuracy.

paragraphs: Bayesian experimental design ranks candidate experiments by their expected information gain: how much observations are expected to change prior beliefs. Computing this quantity can be expensive because it generally requires estimating posterior normalizing constants. Standard sequential Monte Carlo methods devote computation to estimating these constants for individual simulated datasets.

The paper exploits two features of experimental design. Simulated data come with known generating parameters, and the ultimate target is average information gain across datasets. The authors often find that variation across datasets dominates the sampling error within a dataset. This suggests that spending less computation on each individual estimate can be worthwhile.

Reverse-annealed sequential Monte Carlo starts with a single posterior sample and gradually moves backward toward the prior. It trades some additional sampling variance for much lower computational cost. In spring-mass, Johnson-Cook, and source-finding models, the authors demonstrate information-gain estimation using orders of magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations. The efficiency argument depends on the relative contributions of these sources of variance.
neurips-2025-reverse-annealed-sequential.tldr: Reverse-annealed SMC estimates experimental information gain with far fewer likelihood evaluations by starting from one posterior sample and moving toward the prior.

paragraphs: Computational multiplexing captures several cellular structures in one fluorescence image and separates them afterward. A central difficulty is that the structures' relative signal strengths are unknown. Existing decomposition methods are trained at a fixed mixing ratio, which does not reflect the range of intensity combinations encountered in microscopy.

scSplit makes the degree of mixing asymmetry an explicit part of image decomposition. It builds on the iterative image restoration method InDI. A trained regression network estimates the degradation level of the input, and a degradation-specific normalization module uses that information during inference. The decomposition can consequently respond to the estimated mixing conditions of each image.

The authors demonstrate the method on image splitting and bleedthrough removal across five public datasets. These results support its applicability to two relevant microscopy tasks. The key contribution is connecting an estimate of how unevenly signals are mixed to the restoration process, allowing the method to account for varying relative intensities.
neurips-2025-scsplit-bringing-severity-c.tldr: scSplit estimates signal-mixing asymmetry and uses it to adapt fluorescence image separation to varying relative intensities.

paragraphs: Language-model agents often need carefully designed prompts, examples, and task interfaces to perform sequences of decisions. This paper investigates whether agents can improve automatically by reusing their own successful experiences. The method builds a database of completed trajectories and presents them as examples when the agent tackles future tasks.

Even simply accumulating successful trajectories raises performance from 73% to 89% on ALFWorld, 55% to 64% on Wordcraft, and 75% to 79% on InterCode-SQL. In the reported comparisons, those gains exceed upgrading from gpt-4o-mini to gpt-4o and match allowing multiple attempts per task.

The authors further improve the database at two levels. Population-based training propagates collections of examples that perform well, while individual trajectories are retained according to their measured usefulness as demonstrations. With this curation, ALFWorld success reaches 93%, surpassing approaches using stronger models and hand-crafted components. The findings show that selecting and reusing an agent's experience can be a substantial source of improvement.
neurips-2025-self-generated-in-context-e.tldr: Agents improve sequential decision-making by collecting, curating, and reusing their own successful trajectories as in-context examples.

paragraphs: Adversarial training teaches language models to behave safely when given attack prompts, but generating long adversarial suffixes is expensive. This paper studies whether training with shorter suffixes can provide protection against longer ones. It presents a square-root scaling relationship supporting that possibility.

The theoretical analysis concerns linear transformers performing linear regression through in-context learning. Its robust generalization bound depends on the square root of the number of perturbed test examples divided by the number used during training. In this analyzed setting, the result supports training lengths on the order of the square root of the attack length.

Experiments adversarially train open-source language models and test suffix attacks of different lengths. Attack success correlates positively with the corresponding square-root test-length to training-length ratio. The combined evidence supports shorter adversarial training as an efficient defense strategy for suffix attacks. The formal guarantee belongs to the simplified transformer setting, while the language-model results provide empirical evidence for the scaling relationship.
neurips-2025-short-length-adversarial-tr.tldr: Theory in a simplified setting and language-model experiments support using shorter adversarial suffixes in training to defend against longer suffix attacks.

paragraphs: Depthwise separable convolutional networks commonly contain thousands of trained spatial filters. This paper investigates whether much of that apparent variety comes from a very small collection of shared patterns. Through unsupervised searches across architectures and datasets, the authors identify eight candidate universal filters.

Their analysis finds that trained filters are predominantly related to this set through transformations of the form ax+b. The patterns resemble Gaussians, Differences of Gaussians, and their derivatives, connecting them to classical image-processing operators and structures resembling mammalian visual receptive fields. These similarities offer a way to interpret what depthwise layers repeatedly learn.

Networks initialized with the eight unique frozen filters achieve over 80% ImageNet accuracy. On smaller datasets, they can outperform models with thousands of trainable parameters. The findings provide evidence for a compact shared collection of spatial operators and suggest implications for generalization and transfer learning. The universal-filter claim is supported by the reported analysis and experiments across different settings.
neurips-2025-the-quest-for-universal-mas.tldr: The paper identifies eight recurring spatial filters that provide evidence for a compact shared basis in depthwise separable convolutional networks.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning combines contributions from multiple clients, while graph foundation models aim to transfer across domains. Combining them creates an opportunity to use distributed data and computation, but can entangle domain-specific knowledge in representations that are difficult to distinguish. FedGFM+ addresses this problem during initialization and downstream adaptation.

Before pretraining, each client summarizes its graph with domain-specific prototypes. These become semantic anchors around which synthetic embeddings are constructed to initialize the global model. The authors theoretically establish that the prototypes are distinguishable across domains and that this initialization encourages separation of domain knowledge.

During local pretraining, clients also learn lightweight graph prompts capturing their domain preferences. Fine-tuning combines these into an adaptive pool, from which relevant prompts augment the target graph's attributes. Evaluations on eight benchmarks spanning multiple domains and tasks outperform twenty baselines. The results support preserving domain distinctions at both the shared representation level and the later adaptation stage.
neurips-2025-towards-effective-federated.tldr: FedGFM+ uses domain-specific initialization anchors and adaptive prompts to reduce knowledge entanglement in federated graph foundation models.

paragraphs: Video temporal grounding identifies the time interval in a video that matches a natural-language question or description. UniTime applies a generative multimodal language model to this task, aiming to handle complex queries across videos with different viewpoints, genres, and durations. Accurate localization requires connecting visual understanding to explicit time information.

The model interleaves timestamp tokens with video tokens so that temporal information is represented alongside visual content. Training also uses adaptive frame scaling to expose the model to different input granularities. This supports localization in both short and long videos, where the appropriate temporal representation can differ.

Across five public benchmarks, UniTime outperforms leading approaches in both zero-shot and dataset-specific fine-tuned evaluations. It also improves long-form video question answering when used first to retrieve relevant moments. These findings show the value of temporal grounding both as a localization task and as a preliminary step that helps another model focus on relevant video content.
neurips-2025-universal-video-temporal-gr.tldr: UniTime combines explicit timestamp tokens and adaptive frame scaling to locate query-relevant video moments across varied video lengths and domains.

paragraphs: This paper compares neural architectures by how much training data they need, even when computation is unlimited. It studies sequences where each output depends on only a small number q of relevant tokens among N positions. The input prompt specifies those positions, creating a sparse retrieval problem whose relevant locations can change.

For this model, the authors prove that a single-layer Transformer can learn the task if and only if it has at least q attention heads. With enough heads, its sample complexity is almost independent of sequence length. Recurrent networks, by comparison, require a number of samples that grows polynomially with N on the same problem.

A simplified version allows recurrent networks to attain sample complexity almost independent of N, while feedforward networks still require N samples. These results establish a hierarchy for the constructed retrieval settings. They explain how adapting to changing sparse dependencies can create a statistical advantage for attention, beyond questions of what an architecture can represent.
neurips-2025-when-do-transformers-outper.tldr: For specified sparse retrieval tasks, Transformers can require far fewer training samples than recurrent or feedforward networks.
